Cannabis 101

Cannabis for Beginners: Strains, Products and Your First Steps

A plain-language starter guide: what cannabis is, how it became legal in Michigan, how products differ, which gear helps and how to plan your first dispensary visit.

By the High Society teamPublished October 24, 202610 min read

10min readCannabis 101
In this article
  1. What cannabis is
  2. A short history: ancient uses to Michigan's 2018 vote
  3. Medical and adult use today
  4. Indica, sativa, hybrid: handy labels, imperfect predictors
  5. Cannabinoids and terpenes in plain words
  6. Types of cannabis products, from flower to capsules
  7. Gear you may want
  8. Cannabis for beginners: how it affects your body and gentle first formats
  9. Your first visit: ID, questions to ask, starting low
  10. Frequently asked questions

Key takeaways

  • THC causes the high. CBD is not intoxicating in the same way, but it can still make some people drowsy.
  • Indica, sativa and hybrid are loose shorthand; genetic testing published in 2021 found the labels do not reliably track a plant's genetics or ancestry.
  • Smoking or vaping takes effect within minutes, while an edible may take 2 hours to begin and 4 to hit its peak.
  • For a first try, Health Canada points to edibles at or under 2.5 mg of THC, or one or two inhalations of something no stronger than 10% THC.
  • Bring government photo ID to any Michigan dispensary. Adult use starts at 21, medical patients with a card can shop at 18, and ID is checked before every sale.

Cannabis for beginners comes down to a few habits: learn what THC and CBD do, pick one gentle format, keep the first amount small and be patient. Think of this page as cannabis 101 in plain language. It explains what the plant is, how it became legal in Michigan, how product types differ and which gear is worth owning. Then it walks you through a first visit to a dispensary, so you'll know what to ask and what to expect.

What cannabis is

Cannabis is a flowering plant, Cannabis sativa, that people have grown for thousands of years for fiber, seed and its effects on body and mind. Its active compounds are called cannabinoids, and scientists have identified at least 125 of them. Delta-9 THC is the best known, and it's intoxicating: it can briefly change mood, thoughts and perception, which is what people call a high.

Varieties that carry only trace amounts of THC are known as hemp. They're grown mostly for fiber and seed oil, and they won't make you high. Dispensaries sell the intoxicating kind, usually as dried flower buds or as products made from them.

Laws and medical programs often say marijuana, so if you searched for marijuana for beginners, you're in the right place; cannabis is simply the everyday word.

A short history: ancient uses to Michigan's 2018 vote

Cannabis ranks among the oldest crops in East Asia, where it was grown for grain and fiber and used in medicine and ritual. In 2019, archaeologists reported chemical traces of burned cannabis inside wooden braziers from the Jirzankal Cemetery in far western China, dated to around 500 BCE. Those plants were high in psychoactive compounds, a sign that people were seeking out the plant's effects at least 2,500 years ago.

The legal history is much younger. Federal law has listed marijuana as a controlled substance since the Controlled Substances Act of 1970, and as of October 2026, adult-use marijuana is still in Schedule I. Michigan voters have taken their own path twice:

  • 2008: a ballot measure created the state's medical marijuana program.
  • 2018: voters legalized cannabis for adults 21 and older, and the law took effect on December 6, 2018.

Today both markets are licensed and regulated by Michigan's Cannabis Regulatory Agency.

Medical and adult use today

Michigan has two legal lanes, and dispensary signs often mention both:

  • Adult use: anyone 21 or older may buy, possess and use cannabis. The limit for carrying it is 2.5 ounces, and concentrate can make up no more than 15 grams of that total.
  • Medical: registered patients can shop from age 18 with a Michigan medical marijuana card, which requires certification from a Michigan physician.

Some limits apply to everyone. Public consumption is off-limits, and property owners can ban smoking or use on their premises. One exception: a lease can't forbid a tenant from lawfully using cannabis at home by means other than smoking. Driving under the influence is illegal, and there's no numeric THC cutoff, like the 0.08 limit for alcohol, that tells you you're fine to drive. If you're thinking about cannabis for a health reason, start that conversation with a doctor.

Indica, sativa, hybrid: handy labels, imperfect predictors

Menus usually sort products into indica, sativa and hybrid. Shoppers use the terms as shorthand: indica for a heavier, evening feel, sativa for something brighter and hybrids for the space in between.

The science is messier. A team publishing in Nature Plants in 2021 genotyped over 100 cannabis samples, and the "sativa" and "indica" samples showed no genome-wide genetic difference. What the names did correspond to was variation in a handful of terpenes, the compounds that shape aroma.

So use the label as a first clue, then look closer at the THC and CBD numbers, the scent and your own notes on how a product felt. Our breakdown of indica vs. sativa goes further.

Cannabinoids and terpenes in plain words

Cannabinoids do most of the work. Two are worth knowing on day one:

  • THC is intoxicating. It can shift mood, perception and coordination, and it's the first number to check on any label.
  • CBD won't give you a high on its own, yet it isn't free of side effects; some people get drowsy.

Minor cannabinoids like CBN and CBG usually turn up in much smaller amounts.

Terpenes are the aroma compounds, and many of them smell familiar. Limonene gives off a citrus scent, pinene smells like pine, linalool is floral and lavender-like, and caryophyllene recalls black pepper and cloves. Scientists are still sorting out whether terpenes change how cannabis feels, so enjoy them for scent and taste to begin with. Our rundown of common cannabis terpenes walks through the ones you'll see most.

Types of cannabis products, from flower to capsules

Formats differ mainly in how fast they work, how long they last and how precisely you can measure a serving.

ProductWhat it isOnsetGood to know
FlowerDried buds, ground and then smoked or vaporizedSeconds to minutesYou can pace yourself one puff at a time
Pre-rollsJoints that come already rolledSeconds to minutesNo rolling needed, and you can stop whenever you like
VapesCannabis oil in a cartridge that fits a batterySeconds to minutesSo convenient that extra puffs come easily
EdiblesGummies, chocolates and baked goods30 minutes to 2 hoursAdult-use servings in Michigan max out at 10 mg THC
DrinksCannabis-infused beveragesSimilar to ediblesSame 10 mg THC ceiling per serving
ConcentratesWax, shatter and other extractsSeconds to minutesVery potent, so leave them for later
TincturesLiquid extract measured with a dropperVaries with how you take themSmall, adjustable servings
TopicalsLotions and balmsVariesApplied to the skin rather than eaten or inhaled
CapsulesPre-measured oil in a capsuleSimilar to ediblesConsistent servings, slow start

Edibles are also the slowest to peak, sometimes 4 hours after eating, whereas inhaled cannabis tops out within roughly half an hour. Our buyer's guide shows how to compare labels across formats.

At High Society, store menus carry flower, pre-rolls, vape pens, concentrates and edibles, and some also list tinctures and topicals. Stock varies by location and changes often, so pull up your own store's menu before you go.

Gear you may want

Edibles, drinks, tinctures and capsules need no equipment at all. For flower and vapes, a few basics help:

  • Grinder: breaks buds into an even texture, so they roll and burn smoothly.
  • Rolling papers and tips: only if you'd like to roll your own; pre-rolls skip this step.
  • Small pipe: a simple way to take just a puff or two.
  • Vape battery: it has to match your cartridge, so ask before you buy.
  • Lighter or hemp wick, plus storage: a smell-proof container that locks keeps cannabis fresh and away from kids.

Accessories are legal for adults 21 and older to buy, own and use in Michigan. You'll find them on our store menus too; at New Buffalo, papers, lighters and grinders are listed as gear.

Cannabis for beginners: how it affects your body and gentle first formats

Your body runs a cannabinoid signaling network of its own, called the endocannabinoid system. Its parts are receptors, naturally produced cannabinoid messengers, and enzymes that make and dismantle those messengers. THC works by acting on those receptors.

In the short term, people often feel happier or more relaxed. You may also notice time passing strangely, slower thinking and memory, and clumsier movement. Heart rate and blood pressure can go up right after use. Anxiety, fear and even panic become more likely with a big dose, a strong high-THC product or little experience.

That's why your first format matters. Health Canada's lower-risk guidance boils down to two starting points:

  1. Edible: pick one containing 2.5 mg of THC or less, then wait to feel the effects before taking more. An edible can take up to 4 hours to reach its full effect.
  2. Inhaled: stop at one or two puffs of a joint or vape that tests at 10% THC or lower, then wait to feel the effects. Inhaled cannabis can take up to 30 minutes to peak.

Leave alcohol out of the same occasion; the CDC warns that using both together likely brings more impairment than using either one. If you take medication, manage a health condition or are pregnant or breastfeeding, check with your clinician first. For milligram math, see our guide to THC dosing.

Your first visit: ID, questions to ask, starting low

A first dispensary trip is simpler than it might seem. At a High Society store, it goes like this:

  1. Bring ID. A current government photo ID works, and so does a passport. You need to be 21 or older, or 18 or older with a Michigan medical card. Michigan stores check ID before every sale, so expect it each time.
  2. Check in. Our security and front desk team checks you in, and a budtender calls you up when it's your turn.
  3. Say you're new. Our budtenders are happy to slow down and explain the menu.
  4. Ask a few questions. What's the THC per serving, in milligrams? When will I feel it, and for how long? Is there a milder option?
  5. Keep it simple. Pick one product in one format for your first session.
  6. Pay. Cash works; other payment methods depend on the store.

Short on time? Order ahead online, choose a pickup time and ask for curbside if you prefer; you'll get a text once it's ready, and you'll still show ID at pickup. While you're with us, ask about The Society, our free loyalty program. Find a store near you on our dispensary locations page, and read what to expect on a first dispensary trip for more pointers.

Once you're home, keep cannabis in its original packaging, somewhere kids and pets can't reach. Never drive after using it, and don't travel across state lines with cannabis. Take your time, enjoy the experience and keep notes on what you liked. 21+ only. Please consume responsibly.

Frequently asked questions

What's the best way for a beginner to try cannabis?

Start with one gentle format and a small amount, at home, on a day with nowhere to drive. A low-dose edible or a couple of puffs of lower-strength flower are the usual first steps, using the Health Canada starting amounts described above. Then wait. Edibles can be slow, sometimes taking two hours, so resist adding a second serving too soon.

What does cannabis do in the body?

THC binds to cannabinoid receptors, part of the body's endocannabinoid system. Short-term effects can include relaxation or a lift in mood, along with a distorted sense of time, slower thinking and memory, weaker coordination and a faster heartbeat. Bigger doses and stronger products make anxiety or panic more likely. CBD doesn't intoxicate the way THC does, but it can cause drowsiness.

What do I need to bring to a Michigan dispensary?

Bring a government-issued photo ID that hasn't expired, or your passport. Adult-use shoppers must be 21 or older, and medical patients 18 and older also bring their Michigan registry card. Expect an ID check with every purchase, pickup orders included. Cash works at our stores, while other ways to pay differ by location, so check with yours before you go.

How much should a beginner take?

Less than you'd guess. Keep a first edible at or under 2.5 mg of THC, and limit inhaling to a couple of puffs of something rated 10% THC or lower, as Health Canada advises. Edibles keep building for as long as 4 hours, so wait until you feel the full effect before adding more. Increase slowly, and only after a session that felt comfortable.

For adults 21 and older. Keep cannabis away from children and pets, and never drive after consuming. Michigan law does not allow cannabis use in public places.
